text.p: Massimo D'Alema, head of the largest party in Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition government, said on Monday that a mini-budget later this year was inevitable but will not be huge.
"I think it is inevitable that there will be a mini-budget (because of the overshoot)," D'Alema, head of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), told reporters.
He said he did not know how big the mini-budget would be but added: "I don't think it will be a budget of a devastating size.".
He added that it would be "very difficult" for the government to bring forward its full 1998 budget.
Prodi has already said he can not exclude a corrective mini-budget but that it would be modest in size.
The government is due to decide on the mini-budget in the next few weeks.
It has been mulling whether to draft a deficit cutting mini-budget and whether to begin debating next year's budget early.
Prodi and his economic ministers say both would send a strong signal of Italian stability ahead of European Economic and Monetary Union.
Opposition centre-right bloc leader Silvio Berlusconi has offered to work with the coalition on an early 1998 budget in return for a combined assault on welfare reform.
D'Alema, speaking to reporters at the foreign press club, also said that if Italy is left out of EMU, then the country risked "being dramatically broken in two".
Prodi has already said that any mini-budget to compensate for the overshoot would cut spending. This would put his government on a potential collision course with Communist Refoundation.
His coalition depends on the hard-left party for its majority in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house). -- Rome newsroom +396-678-2501
